final_answer:
The sunk cost fallacy occurs when decisions are influenced by prior investments—time, money, or effort—rather than current and future value.  

1) **Business**: A company spends millions on an app that fails to gain traction. Instead of pivoting or canceling, executives justify continued funding because “we’ve already invested so much.” The fallacy is ignoring future returns and clinging to past expenditure.  

2) **Personal**: Someone stays in a draining relationship or job because they “put in so much time.” They rationalize staying, even if the future seems worse, simply to avoid “wasting” earlier effort.  

3) **Public policy**: A government pours more funds into a construction project that’s chronically delayed and over budget, arguing, “we’ve already committed so many resources.” This ignores whether the project will ever deliver value versus the ongoing costs.  

In all cases, the key mistake is treating past costs as relevant to future decisions, rather than focusing on what’s best moving forward.
